item.title: The biggest misread of anyone predicting the end of software engineering was imagining that the world only needed a certain amount of software, and bringing automation to the field would reduce the need for labor. Exactly the opposite is happening where essentially most things are actually turning...
item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
The biggest misread of anyone predicting the end of software engineering was imagining that the world only needed a certain amount of software, and bringing automation to the field would reduce the need for labor.
Exactly the opposite is happening where essentially most things are actually turning into software. Because agents can use tools, work with computers, write software on the fly, and process data like humans (but far faster), we can now throw “software” at problems that never could reasonably be digitized before.
What that leads to is the role of engineering taking on greater importance in the economy, because we can now engineer far more systems and processes than were possible before.
If you’re a bank trying to do new forms of trading, engineers are often your first bet. If you are in life sciences, you expect more and more research and lab work to be engineering centric. If you’re in manufacturing, you’re trying to automate more of the supply chain, all that is engineering. More and more work is shaped like software problems.
Yes we’re not going to be coding manually in the future. But almost everything will be code, which means those that understand it are in a fantastic position.

作者：Peter Yang 账号：@petergyang 简介：Practical AI tutorials and interviews for busy people | Get my best AI skills and guides at https://t.co/6VAA6p81x6
If you have way too many apps and agents (45!) connected to your Google account like me, here's a prompt to audit and remove them:
"Help me audit my Google app connections at https://t.co/5eMX9dNhLD
1. Review EVERY app across all connection categories. Ask me which ones I still use rather than guessing.
2. Open each app's details. Distinguish basic Google sign-in from permissions to access Gmail, Drive, Calendar, or other data.
3. Suggest which to keep, disconnect, or ask me about. Explain your reasoning and what might stop working. Flag broad permissions, unfamiliar providers, and duplicate entries.
4. Show me your recommendations before changing anything. Only disconnect apps I explicitly approve, then verify they're removed. Don't delete app accounts or cancel subscriptions.”

item.title: What Happens When Billions of AI Agents Hit Your Database? (Andy Pavlo)
item.description:
播客：The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:06 What is a file system? It's a database. Right? Everything's a database. Every month, there's a story where someone lost their production database because the agent deleted something.
Speaker 1 | 00:06 - 00:15 It's the wild west for people that don't know their history databases. It's just like, you know, taking a cheetah, giving them much cocaine, and putting it a Ferrari. Like, the amount of speed that people are developing these things is insane.
Speaker 2 | 00:16 - 00:38 That is Andy Pavlo. In the world of databases, Andy is about as close to a god as it gets. The Carnegie Mellon professor whose courses taught an entire generation of engineers about databases, and as it turns out, the AI models too. Andy recently made some waves by joining ClickHouse to found ClickHouse Labs. Now not long ago, databases in AI meant vector search and rag.
Speaker 2 | 00:38 - 00:52 But today, agents create databases, write to them, and sometimes even delete them. Welcome to databases in the age of agents. I'm Matt Turk, and this is the MAD Podcast. Andy, welcome.
Speaker 1 | 00:52 - 00:53 Hey, Matt. How are you doing, man?
Speaker 2 | 00:53 - 01:01 Good. I'm excited to talk about all things AI agents, databases. Larry Ellison, we have two, and then, Wu Tang Clan.
Speaker 1 | 01:01 - 01:10 Oh, we definitely do Wu Tang Clan. Do we have to talk about Larry Ellison? I mean, it's like a little early to come out of the gate. Although it's... Is hilarious because he's like the supervillain with databases.
Speaker 1 | 01:10 - 01:11 Like, he owns a Hawaiian island.
Speaker 2 | 01:11 - 01:13 Well, that seems to be working out for him.
Speaker 1 | 01:13 - 01:13 Yes.
Speaker 2 | 01:13 - 01:17 Alright. We can graduate, to talking about Larry Ellison later in the conversation.
Speaker 1 | 01:17 - 01:21 I will say my contract with ClickHouse does allow me to talk about Larry Ellison. I made sure that was in writing.
Speaker 2 | 01:21 - 01:41 Alright. Awesome. I want to take it from, the the top. So two years ago, the topic of databases and AI came up. There was a whole era of vector databases and this whole idea that you need to do RAG in connection with chatbot searches.
Speaker 2 | 01:41 - 01:54 That was kind of two years ago. I think a lot of people's mental models kind of, like, stopped there in terms of, like, this intersection of databases and AI. Clearly, are in the age of agents now. How is that different? What does that change?
Speaker 1 | 01:54 - 02:32 Obviously, the vector databases, although you're right that like the... In terms of like being in the zeitgeist of AI and databases, you know, probably two years ago is when the rag vector data sort of came into play. But the vector databases themselves, like a lot of them were around since like 2016. It's just now that like the use for them became obvious because you can use them to enhance and improve agents doing things. So I think vector database market is interesting because they were early in the in the space, but but they were really pushing the idea that you wanna do this, you know, a...
Speaker 1 | 02:32 - 02:58 The approximate similarity search on vectors or embeddings instead of doing an exact search that the database systems have traditionally done. And this helps too when you're dealing with natural languages that where the the semantics maybe what what you're trying to look for or query against isn't... You can't precisely define. Like, find me all the the albums in in, you know, from from artists in New York City that talk about doing, you know, certain certain kind of activities. Right?
Speaker 1 | 02:58 - 03:33 It's very hard to define exactly what that is. And the the the magic of approximate nearest neighbor search where these vector embedding searches in a vector database is that you can you can look up things based on the semantics of of the thing you're looking for and just sort of... It works out that way because you're not trying to do exact keyword searches. So when, you know, Chat2B blew up in 2024, 2023, when again, when everyone became aware that this is this is now a technology that exists, the vector databases were in the right position at the right time because they they could augment and improve these these chatbots. But like the the moat, if you will, wasn't that big.
Speaker 1 | 03:33 - 03:46 At the end of the day, it's just an index. And within a year, pretty much every single database vendor had their own vector index. And now it's become sort of standard stable takes... Table stakes. Like every data system that everybody's using has their own vector index.
Speaker 1 | 03:46 - 04:09 Now it doesn't say that the vector data says can't do certain things better than what the, you know, a traditional data system could do. It's just now that everyone has this... That basic functionality. So I think that you still use vector searches to enhance and improve the chat bots or the agents now. It's just the you don't need to have a specialized one database that can only do that.
Speaker 2 | 04:09 - 04:31 And agents, now, create databases, use databases, can make changes to databases. So maybe a year ago when Databricks acquired Neon, there was this stat, that I believe said that, the number, or the percentage of agents creating Neon databases went from 30% to 80%.
Speaker 1 | 04:31 - 04:35 But the databases created by agents was like larger than anything else.
Speaker 2 | 04:35 - 04:42 Unpack that for us. What does that mean? An agent creating a database? Why does an agent need to create a database in the first place?
Speaker 1 | 04:42 - 05:26 The creation of a database and then there's branching of an existing database and I think the Databricks metric was about like the branches being created by agents. So what does branching mean? So branching is when you have a database system or sorry, a database and you want to make a sort of copy on write snapshot of that that database and have it look like two unique databases. And the reason why you wanna do that is you could have your production database that's running your your business, your application, like, where all your your you know, the system of record, all your changes are going into. But then you wanna have either a human developer or an agent be able to start trying out new things, make changes to the application, and you want them to operate on the real database.
Speaker 1 | 05:27 - 06:06 Because oftentimes, traditionally, you would make copies of the database or have a smaller version of the of the database, like a sample of what would already exist there because it's just too expensive to to copy things around. So you have like a staging or development database, and then you would then hopefully apply your changes to the production database and you hope things that once you go to a larger scale, everything works out. So what branching allows you to do is it allows you to make a snapshot of the real database, have all the changes that you make go to the snapshot and not affect the production database. And once you're okay with the changes you've made, maybe not necessarily the data, but it's usually for like the schema or the application code. Once you know you've vetted it on the snapshot, then you can put it live in the production database.
Speaker 1 | 06:06 - 06:32 So now with these agents, people are spinning up, these coding agents to write new features, write new new parts of their application. It's not something humans are doing anymore. And now you wanna have these agents, you know, they wanna they wanna vet their changes on a copy of the database so you can create branches on these things. Often, it just shows up when you're running testing as well. Like a lot of times, the the the branches are created by, you know, PRs running and GitHub actions or testing things like that.
Speaker 1 | 06:32 - 06:50 You want to run your tester code on a copy of the database rather than the live o...
